title: On Early Detection of Hallucinations in Factual Question Answering

problem.claim: Hallucinations in large language model generations impede user trust.

gap.claim: Fluent and coherent hallucinated generations make detection difficult.

contributions.claim: The work probes input token attributions, output Softmax probabilities, and internal self-attention and fully-connected-layer activations for signs of hallucinations in open-ended question answering.
It trains binary classifiers using generation artifacts as features to classify generations as hallucinated or non-hallucinated.
Tokens preceding a hallucination can predict the subsequent hallucination before it occurs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The distributions of the examined generation artifacts tend to differ between hallucinated and non-hallucinated generations.
The hallucination classifiers achieve up to 0.80 AUROC.

narrative_sequence.summary: Hallucinations undermine user trust, and their fluent presentation makes detection difficult.
The work examines input, output, and internal model artifacts for hallucination signals.
Artifact distributions differ across hallucinated and non-hallucinated generations.
Binary classifiers using these artifacts reach up to 0.80 AUROC.
Preceding tokens can predict a later hallucination before it occurs.
